tip: yn (in) plus Caernarfon gives yng Nghaernarfon: c changes to ngh and yn becomes yng before it.
fy (my) nasal-mutates the next word: pwysedd becomes fy mhwysedd, p changing to mh.
Before an m sound, yn (in) becomes ym: pobman turns into ym mhobman, p mutating to mh.
After pum (five), blynedd becomes mlynedd: pum mlynedd. Some numbers nasal-mutate the following noun.
gyda (with) adds a breath after p: plant becomes gyda phlant, p changing to ph.
ei meaning her adds an h in spelling: plant becomes ei phlant; ei meaning his would give ei blant instead.
o (from) softens the next word: Pontypridd becomes o Bontypridd, p turning into b.
An adjective softens after a feminine noun: miniog becomes finiog in cyllell finiog (sharp knife).
Welsh has no verb for have: Mae gen i brofiad is literally there is with me experience, meaning I have experience.
Feelings sit on you: Mae hiraeth dwfn arna i means I feel a deep longing, where arna i is ar (on) plus me.
ers marks time still ongoing: ers deng mlynedd means for ten years and counting, up to now.
mynd dan fy nghroen literally means going under my skin, the set phrase for something that irritates you.
The ending -af makes the most: hir (long) becomes hiraf (longest) in yr afon hiraf.
Dyma means here is or this is, pointing at what is in front of you: Dyma'r traeth, this is the beach.
The ending -odd marks a past he or she: canu becomes Canodd hi (she sang).
Buon ni means we were, the plain past of bod (to be); the -on ni ending is the we part.
Paid â tells one person not to do something: Paid â rhoi'r gorau means don't give up.
The ending -wch gives a polite or plural command: yfed (to drink) becomes Yfwch (drink).
